# Exact discrete certificates and a product rule for tripod packings

For distinct apices$p,q$, their positive closed coordinate tripods are disjoint exactly when$p_i<q_i$ in at least two coordinates or$p_i>q_i$ in at least two. This is the source's pairwise2-comparability formulation. The exact endpoint convention matters: replacing strict comparisons by weak ones would allow coincident rays.

If all three coordinates differ, two arms cannot meet: two coordinate rays in three dimensions have at least one jointly fixed coordinate, which would have to agree. One of the two comparison directions then wins at least two coordinates. If exactly one coordinate agrees, relabel it as$z$. Disjointness holds precisely when the$x,y$ differences are both strict and have the same sign. Opposite signs cause the positive$x$-arm of one tripod to meet the positive$y$-arm of the other. If two coordinates agree, the remaining same-direction rays overlap. This exhausts every case and proves the equivalence.

Here is an explicit construction with$s^3$ apices in$[s^2]^3$. For$a,b,c\in[s]$, take
\[
(x,y,z)=((a-1)s+b,\ (b-1)s+c,\ (c-1)s+a).
\]
Distinct index triples give distinct apices. If all three index differences are nonzero, their three leading-coordinate signs determine the resulting coordinate signs, so one direction wins two. If exactly one differs, it changes two displayed coordinates in the same direction. If exactly two differ, equal signs give two leading-coordinate wins; opposite signs give a tie in those two leading signs, resolved by the third displayed coordinate, whose lower-order term has one of those signs. In every case two strict coordinate comparisons agree. Thus the tripods are pairwise disjoint and$F(s^2)\ge s^3$, giving$F(n)\ge\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor^3$ for all$n$.

More generally,$F(nm)\ge F(n)F(m)$. For valid apex sets$A\subset[n]^3$ and$B\subset[m]^3$, use triples with coordinates$m(a_i-1)+b_i$. If outer triples differ, their two strict agreeing comparisons dominate any difference between inner digits; if they agree, use the valid inner pair. The representation by outer and inner digits is unique. Iteration amplifies any exact finite lower certificate into an infinite family; it does not prove that a heuristic finite candidate is valid.

There is also a useful one-way graph reduction, recorded in the primary source. Make a bipartite graph with two copies of$[n]$ and edge$(y,z)$ for each apex$(x,y,z)$, colored$x$. The projection to$(y,z)$ is injective, since equal$y,z$ would make two tripods overlap. A color class is a matching with its edges strictly increasing in both coordinates. It is induced: if$(i,y_1,z_1),(i,y_2,z_2)$ have$y_1<y_2,z_1<z_2$, a cross apex$(j,y_1,z_2)$ would require$j>i$ to compare with the first and$j<i$ to compare with the second. The other cross edge gives the same contradiction. Thus induced-matching upper bounds transfer to$F(n)$; arbitrary induced-matching constructions need not satisfy the stricter coordinate comparisons, so their lower bounds do not transfer automatically.

Pairwise comparability is not a global order: $(1,2,3),(2,3,1),(3,1,2)$ form a directed comparison cycle while all their tripods are disjoint. Arguments assuming transitivity would wrongly discard valid packings. The exact asymptotic exponent remains undetermined by these constructions and reductions.
